 Print this Article 
 View Comments Rays reliever Cam Booser entered the World Series with no runs allowed in six appearances this postseason. David J. Phillip/AP Photo/David J. Phillip E very player in the World Series has a story to tell. But none quite like Tampa Bay lefthander Cam Booser . 
 His road to the Fall Classic took Booser through five major league organizations, three colleges, two independent teams, and one retirement. 
 Along the way, the 34-year-old had two elbow surgeries and another on his shoulder. He also was hit by a car while riding his bicycle in spring training in 2015, injuring his back. 
 Booser retired two years later to take a construction job, then returned to baseball in 2021 after trying to throw again and realizing his arm didn’t hurt. 
 The Red Sox signed him before the 2023 season, and he made his major league debut in April 2024 . 
 He has since posted a 3.45 ERA in 124 regular-season games for the Red Sox, White Sox, and Rays. Booser made six scoreless appearances in Tampa Bay’s first nine postseason games, retiring 14 of the 17 batters he faced. He allowed only one hit, a single. 
 Get 108 Stitches Receive the Globe's best reporting and commentary on the Red Sox every weekday. Enter Email Sign Up “It’s unbelievable, man. I don’t know how else to say it, but it’s a true blessing and a dream come true,” Booser told the Globe. “This year has been a perfect fit since the first day of spring training. 
 “I’ve gotten along with every player, staff member, clubby, chef. Everybody in this organization is phenomenal. An unbelievable fit. I’m very, very grateful to be here.” 
 Cam Booser's first 43 major league appearances came as a member of the 2024 Red Sox. Matthew J. Lee/Globe Staff He also credits the Red Sox for spotting him pitching for the Lancaster Barnstormers of the independent Atlantic League in 2022. 
 “If it wasn’t for Craig Breslow giving me a chance, I probably wouldn’t be here,” Booser said. “Maybe I just spend another year in Triple-A and who knows where I am today? 
 “I’ll always be incredibly grateful to Mr. Breslow and to the Sox organization for giving me a shot. Not only did they give me a shot to go play in the big leagues, but they took a shot on a 31-year-old when nobody else would. So I’m incredibly grateful to the Red Sox. They gave me the shot to make my dream come true.” 
 Related : Lexington’s Sal Frelick and his small-market Brewers look to upend expectations and win their first World Series Booser said the Sox coaches, Andrew Bailey in particular, helped him better understand how best to use his pitches. 
 “Bailey switched my sweeper grip, and that helped me a lot,” he said. “But it was showing me that my cutter was one of my best pitches, and I needed to throw it a lot more. That really made a difference.” 
 Booser had a 3.38 ERA in 43 games for the Sox. But the organization was deep in lefthanded relief options, and Booser was traded to the White Sox after the season for Yhoiker Fajardo , an 18-year-old righthander. 
 Fajardo pitched well, then was spun off to the Cardinals in the trade for Willson Contreras last winter. 
 The Rays signed Booser as a free agent two weeks before spring training this season. He was in Triple-A until June 2, then had a 1.98 ERA over 42 games. 
 Related : When Rays or Brewers win World Series, a former PawSox announcer will be on the call “I don’t know where we’d be without his contributions this year,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “He’s pitched with so much confidence. I think he’s a better pitcher now than he was in spring training. 
 “The velocity he’s shown, he’s always been able to show it. But to be able to sustain it like he has this year is really, really impressive. He’s gotten a ton of big outs already, and we’re going to need him to get some more.” 
 It all goes back to the Red Sox giving Booser a chance. 
 “I loved my time in Boston,” he said. “Pitching at Fenway was special. Every time I go back there, I have a lot of appreciation for what they did for me. Now I’m at the World Series.” 
 FINISHING SCHOOL
 Red Sox lose another executive
 The Athletics hiring 31-year-old Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith as their new president of baseball operations speaks to how highly the industry regards the organization. 
 Smith led the research and development department. The Athletics also considered assistant GM Mike Groopman . Thirteen months ago, the Nationals hired Paul Toboni as their baseball chief. His background was in scouting and player development. 
 Credit to Breslow for having a knack for spotting front-office talent. Now he has another spot to fill. 
 Oddly, the Sox had four assistant general managers on their executive depth chart last season, but no actual general manager. When he was hired three years ago, Breslow said he intended to hire a GM. That talk has disappeared over the last year. Breslow does have a chief of staff, Matt Sauers . 
 The Brewers, Dodgers, Rays, and Yankees are among the teams that have hired former chief executives as senior advisers. World Series-winning executives Theo Epstein , Ben Cherington , and Dave Dombrowski were big believers in that model, but the Sox have moved away from it since Chaim Bloom took over in 2019. 
 Whether that’s a personal preference or the Sox not wanting to budget for such a position isn’t clear. 
 Smith joined the Sox before the 2025 season after spending seven years with the Rays. He maintained a low public profile with both organizations, never consenting to any interviews. How he handles the public relations aspects of the job remains to be seen. But the Athletics hired Smith for his ability to use data in constructing a winning team. 
 Smith is the youngest president of baseball operations in the league. Toboni, 36, held that title for one year. 
 “The world is run by 31-year-olds today,” Athletics owner John Fisher said Wednesday when introducing Smith in Las Vegas. 
 A few other observations on the Red Sox: 
 ⋅ Payton Tolle was in Milwaukee on Thursday and Friday as a World Series correspondent for Major League Baseball. He appeared on MLB Network interviewing players and on the league’s social media channels. 
 One of his duties was taking in the tailgate scene at American Family Field before Game 1. 
 “It’s a fun thing,” said Tolle, who carried a custom microphone with his photo pasted on the side. “The league asked me about doing something, and I thought it would be a good experience. You know me, I’m always up for something like this.” 
 Recently retired Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas and Blue Jays infielder Ernie Clement also will be correspondents during the Series. 
 ⋅ Righthander Johan Oviedo , who appeared in only one game this past season, has become a regular visitor to Aroldis Chapman’s home gym in Florida. 
 Oviedo, 28, has a world of ability but has pitched only 44 major league innings over the last three seasons. He missed all of 2024 recovering from Tommy John surgery, then had a 3.57 ERA in nine starts for the Pirates in 2025. 
 The Sox traded well-regarded outfield prospect Jhostynxon Garcia to Pittsburgh as part of a five-player deal to land Oviedo. He made one relief appearance in March, then missed the rest of the season with an elbow strain and had several setbacks along the way. 
 Tyron Guerrero , a journeyman reliever, flourished last season after working with Chapman. Oviedo could be next to make that jump. 
 Nestor Cortes (Phillies), Nabil Crismatt (free agent), Freddy Fermin (Padres), Andrés Machado (free agent), and Salvador Perez (Royals) also have been part of the workout group. 
 Chapman’s gym is a converted garage loaded with equipment. 
 ⋅ Kurt Suzuki , who was fired by the Angels after one season as manager, could emerge as a good candidate for the Sox coaching staff. 
 For now, Bailey is the only coach with any major league playing experience. Suzuki played parts of 16 seasons in the majors and appeared in 19 postseason games. He was a teammate of Bailey and Breslow with the Athletics from 2009-11. 
 ⋅ Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela were among the winners of the well-respected Fielding Bible Awards . Rafaela also won last year, while Abreu won in 2024. 
 Rafaela was selected as the center fielder. But Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong was selected as the defensive player of the year, with Rafaela second and Abreu third. 
 Huh? 
 Both players received eight first-place votes, seven second-place votes, and two third-place votes from the panel in the center-field balloting. Rafaela won on a statistical tiebreaker. But in a separate vote, Crow-Armstrong was selected as the overall best. 
 ETC.
 Too much of a good thing?
 It’s hard to argue with the success Major League Baseball has had with rule changes in recent years. 
 In 2023 , the pitch timer sped up the pace of play, and stolen bases climbed dramatically after pitchers were limited to two disengagements from the rubber per plate appearance. 
 Fans also have come to enjoy the ABS challenges and the added layer of strategy they bring to the game. 
 Now the league is experimenting with limits on how far outfielders can shift. 
 In Arizona Fall League games at Salt River Fields in Scottsdale, outfielders must position themselves in a certain spot before the pitch. The center fielder is essentially straight up, with the corner infielders closer to the foul lines and shallower than usual. 
 Outfielders must stand within a few feet of a mark on the field. An auxiliary scoreboard tells the players and fans if the outfielders are legally positioned. 
 The idea is to create more balls in the gap. But outfielders could also be better positioned to catch what would be bloop singles. 
 MLB considered outfield positioning rules several years ago and decided against it after some experimentation. There is no indication such a rule would come to the highest level — or even the full-season minor leagues — any time soon. 
 It’s understandable that the league would want more offense. But punishing teams who develop athletic defensive players doesn’t seem right, either. 
 If outfielders become less of a factor defensively, teams could be encouraged to use more slow-footed DH types in the corners. That doesn’t improve the game’s aesthetics. 
 And how many scoreboards is everybody supposed to keep track of? 
 Extra bases 
 Depending on how long the World Series lasts, teams will have roughly a month to sign free agents to major league contracts and make trades before the expected lockout takes effect on Dec. 1. “I wish I knew,” said one executive when asked if he expected a lot of activity. “But you get only so many bites of the apple. So if something matches up, you can always deal with the consequences later.” The free agent class is thin outside of Tarik Skubal , Michael King (who will presumably opt out of his contract with the Padres), Randy Arozarena , Seiya Suzuki , and Brandon Lowe . Skubal is represented by Scott Boras , who traditionally waits out the market. The GM Meetings start Nov. 9 in Las Vegas. For teams with clear needs, that will be an opportunity to strike instead of waiting for the frenzy after a new collective bargaining agreement is in place. For the Red Sox, who need more power in their lineup, acting sooner rather than later could make sense . . . The Yankees have gone 17 seasons since their last World Series victory despite making the postseason 13 times. But Brian Cashman will be back for a 30th season as general manager, and Aaron Boone for his 10th year as manager. Cashman agreed to a new contract last week. Boone enters the final year of his deal. Owner Hal Steinbrenner , who took questions from reporters via Zoom on Wednesday, refreshingly blamed the players for the team’s offensive slide this season. “The bottom line is the players didn’t live up to their end of the bargain in the playoffs,” he said. That’s true, but that doesn’t mean hitting coach James Rowson is safe . . . Brewers owner Mark Attanasio has twice done press conferences during the postseason this year, both times joined by president of baseball operations Matt Arnold . He feels it’s important. “The media is essential for us to be able to communicate with our fans,” he said on Thursday. “We can get 40,000 people into the ballpark here, but we want to communicate to millions of people around the country who are fans of our team. I think it helps to hear from the owner as well as just the manager or the head of baseball ops.” . . . John Mozeliak had an interesting four months. The longtime Cardinals executive came out of retirement and joined the Angels to run baseball operations on an interim basis in mid-June after general manager Perry Minasian was fired. He traded outfielder Jo Adell , catcher Logan O’Hoppe , and righthanded relievers Chase Silseth , José Soriano , and Ryan Zeferjahn at the trade deadline and appeared to be putting the organization on a good course to rebuild. Mozeliak seemed prepared to stay on the job until Arte Moreno sold the team to Stan Kroenke in September . Now he will exit when his contract expires in December … Boston College has had only one player taken in the first three rounds of the draft over the last five seasons. Julio Solier could change that. The shortstop from Springfield Central wowed scouts with a 390-foot homer against UConn in a fall ball game this month. He hit .354 with a .932 OPS last season and stole 28 bases. That led to an invitation to train with Team USA and eight games with Harwich in the Cape League. Solier had 15 doubles and five triples for the Eagles last season but only three home runs. His 6-foot, 200-pound frame suggests there’s more power to be had . . . Righthander Dylan Cunningham of Austin Prep in Reading has committed to Virginia ahead of his junior season. The Cavaliers recruited him as a two-way player. Cunningham, who is from Peabody, is recovering from Tommy John surgery and could be limited to hitting this season. Catcher Bradley McCafferty , who graduated from Austin Prep last spring, is at Virginia . . . Braves assistant general manager Ben Sestanovich is a candidate to replace Dana Brown as Astros GM. Sestanovich played at Harvard from 2008-11. He interned in the Padres front office in 2010 and rose to director of player development before joining the Braves in 2019. One red flag with the Astros job is how much influence Jeff Bagwell has on owner Jim Crane in major roster decisions . . . Not to make any of you feel too old, but Pedro Martinez turns 55 on Sunday. He was 117-37 with a 2.52 ERA for the Red Sox from 1998-2004 and won two Cy Young Awards. His Hall of Fame plaque includes the line, “The fiery righty from the Dominican Republic owned the inside part of the plate with an exploding fastball and confounding changeup.” Martinez won the pitching Triple Crown in 1999, leading the league in wins (23), ERA (2.07), and strikeouts (313). Cy Young of the 1901 Boston Americans is the only other pitcher in franchise history to accomplish that feat.
